newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian court orders NNPC to insure with state.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian court orders NNPC to insure with state.

text.p: A Nigerian court has ordered state-owned Nigerian National Petroleum Corp (NNPC) to insure its assets with state insurer NICON.
The court was ruling on Monday in a suit brought last month by six Nigerian firms contesting who should control NNPC's lucrative insurance account worth 2.025 billion naira.
Federal high court judge Justice Mahmud Belgore said: "NICON only should insure and reinsure all the NNPC assets for 1997."
"The insurance and reinsurance brokers used by NICON in previous years before the present dispute should be used for the next one year," he added.

National Insurance Corporation of Nigeria (NICON) is 100 percent federal government-owned and is the biggest insurance firm in Nigeria. It announced this year a doubling of its capital base to a billion naira and after tax profit increase of 43 percent to 813 million naira.
NNPC, also 100 percent owned by the federal government, pumps two million barrels of crude oil daily, which accounts for more than 90 percent of Nigeria's foreign exchange earnings.
It assets include oil refineries, petrocheimcal plants, oil depots and sundry other properties.

"It might amount to criminal irresponsibility and insensitivity to national interests to allow the mainstay of the country's economy go unprotected and left under risk which will result in calamitous consequences," Belgore said.
Two of the six feuding firms -- Fidelity Bond of Nigeria and Trinity Mills Insurance Brokers -- said NICON brokered their appointment which entitled them to receive commissions.

Lawyers for Fidelity Bond and Trinity Mills had also wanted the court to stop the transfer of the account to the four other firms -- UNIC Insurance, Industrial and General Insurance Company Limited, Inter-Continental Insurance Company Limited and Kapital Insurance Company Nigeria Limited.
All six companies are 100 percent Nigerian-owned.
Belgore ruled that NNPC and oil minister Dan Etete had no right to transfer the state oil company's account to any other insurance firm.
